mainEntity.name: How long does composite bonding typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: Composite bonding can last anywhere from three to ten or more years, though this varies considerably between patients. The location of the bonding, the size of the restoration, the patient's bite, and their maintenance habits all influence longevity. There is no universally guaranteed lifespan — individual outcomes depend on clinical factors that can only be properly assessed during a dental examination. Regular reviews help patients understand the current condition of their bonding and any steps that may help support it over time.

mainEntity.name: Can composite bonding be repaired if it chips?

acceptedAnswer.text: In many cases, yes. One of the practical advantages of composite resin as a material is that minor chips or surface wear can often be repaired by adding and reshaping additional composite, rather than replacing the entire restoration. Whether repair is appropriate depends on the extent and location of the damage, the condition of the underlying tooth, and the adhesion of the remaining composite. Your dental professional can assess the restoration clinically and advise on the most appropriate course of action.

mainEntity.name: Does whitening toothpaste affect composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some whitening toothpastes have a higher abrasive content, which over time may affect the surface smoothness of composite resin. A rougher surface can be more prone to staining. Patients with composite bonding are often advised to choose low-abrasivity toothpastes. Your dental team can recommend suitable products based on your individual situation. It is also worth noting that tooth whitening treatments — including bleaching gels — do not change the colour of composite resin, which can lead to a mismatch if whitening is undertaken after bonding is placed.

mainEntity.name: Should I avoid certain foods after composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: In the immediate period following treatment, your dental team may recommend avoiding very hard foods that could stress the newly placed composite before it has fully settled. In the longer term, there is no strict list of foods to avoid entirely, but moderating the frequency of highly staining drinks (such as coffee, tea, and red wine) and acidic beverages may help maintain the appearance and surface quality of the bonding. Practical measures, such as using a straw for cold drinks or rinsing with water after meals, are commonly suggested.

mainEntity.name: Does teeth grinding affect composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, bruxism (habitual tooth grinding or clenching) can place significantly increased mechanical load on composite bonding, which may accelerate wear or increase the risk of chipping. If you know you grind your teeth, or if your dental team identifies signs consistent with bruxism, it is important to discuss this before or alongside composite bonding treatment. A custom-made occlusal splint (nightguard) can help protect both natural teeth and restorations during sleep, and may be recommended as part of your overall dental management plan.

mainEntity.name: How often should I see my dentist after having composite bonding?

acceptedAnswer.text: General guidance is to attend dental check-ups at the frequency recommended by your dental professional, which for most patients is every six to twelve months. Patients with composite bonding may benefit from professional polishing at hygiene appointments, as this helps maintain the surface smoothness of the composite. Your dental team may recommend a specific review schedule based on your individual oral health and the nature of your bonding. If you notice any changes to your bonding between appointments — such as roughness, chipping, or sensitivity — it is always appropriate to contact your practice rather than wait.
